definition: ACROSS is a Singular Strategic R&D Project led by Treelogic funded by the Spanish Ministry of Industry, Tourism and Trade activities in the field of Robotics and Cognitive Computing over an execution time-frame from 2009 to 2011.
details: ACROSS project involves a number higher than 100 researchers from 13 Spanish entities.

explainer.lead: ACROSS was a Spanish government-funded research project that tried to make robots less like vending machines and more like adaptable helpers. Running from 2009 to 2011, it brought together over 100 researchers from 13 organizations to build robots that could learn, reconfigure themselves, and be updated remotely.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a robot that doesn't just do one chore it's programmed for, but can figure out new ways to help as situations change. ACROSS was like a big team project where scientists built robots that could learn on their own and be fixed or upgraded from far away, kind of like how your phone gets software updates. They tested these robots helping people with disabilities, kids with autism, and even as friendly greeters in stores.
tiers.practitioner: ACROSS produced an open-source framework for social robotics with three deployment targets: assistive living (daily task support), therapeutic intervention (autism spectrum cognitive support), and human-robot interaction in commercial settings. The architecture emphasized remote software access and autonomous behavioral reconfiguration rather than hard-coded service loops. Practitioners should note the project concluded in 2011; its open-source services may require significant modernization for current ROS or similar middleware stacks.
tiers.paperLevel: ACROSS (2009–2011) was a Singular Strategic R&D Project led by Treelogic and funded by the Spanish Ministry of Industry, Tourism and Trade. The project framework posited social robotics as requiring self-reconfigurable intelligent systems capable of autonomous behavioral modification through understanding, learning, and software remote access, moving beyond predefined service provision. Deliverables included open-source services and application prototypes across autonomous living, psycho-affective disorder intervention, and marketing domains. No originating peer-reviewed publication or formal algorithmic specification is named in available sources.

explainer.example: A robot placed in a home to help a person with mobility limitations might initially know only basic commands. Over weeks, it learns the person's daily routines—when they typically need water, which rooms they frequent, how they gesture for help. When researchers develop a better voice-recognition module, they push it to the robot overnight. The robot now understands slurred speech it couldn't before, without anyone visiting the house.

explainer.intuition: Most robots are built like appliances: they do exactly what they were built for and nothing else. ACROSS asked what if a robot could reshape its own abilities after deployment, learning from people and receiving new skills over the internet like a phone updating its apps.
howItWorks: A robot starts with basic social interaction capabilities rather than a fixed service script
The system observes and understands its environment and human users, building models of what people need
Through learning algorithms, it autonomously modifies its own behavior to better serve those needs
Engineers can remotely access and reconfigure the robot's software, pushing updates or new capabilities without physical intervention
The resulting behaviors are offered through open-source services that other researchers can adapt and extend
explainer.whyItMatters: ACROSS anticipated a shift in robotics that is now mainstream: the move from closed, single-purpose machines to open, updatable platforms. Its emphasis on remote reconfiguration and open-source collaboration prefigured later cloud robotics and robot-as-a-service models, while its focus on assistive and therapeutic applications addressed genuine social needs.
misconceptions: ACROSS built a single robot model; in fact it was a collaborative framework across multiple institutions with varied hardware
The project produced commercial products; it was a 2009–2011 research initiative with open-source outputs, not a product line
The robots were fully autonomous from the start; the framework emphasized learning and reconfiguration over time, not immediate unsupervised operation
